study.title: As the deer pants for streams of water.
study.intro: Eleven verses give voice to a worshiper far from the temple, thirsting for God, remembering festival crowds, and answering despair with a repeated refrain of hope.
study.context: The heading calls this a Maskil of the sons of Korah, a Levitical family of temple singers. Psalms 42 and 43 share a refrain (42:5, 42:11, 43:5) and are often read as one poem in three stanzas; Psalm 43 has no heading of its own, which supports that reading. The speaker is in the far north near the Jordan's sources and Mount Hermon (42:6), cut off from the Jerusalem sanctuary, and taunted with 'Where is your God?' (42:3, 42:10). The psalm opens Book Two of the Psalter (Psalms 42–72), where 'God' (Elohim) is used far more often than the covenant name. The Scripture is loaded unchanged from the bundled BSB, including the heading.
study.peopleNote: The sons of Korah are named in the heading as the singers or collectors of this Maskil. Their profile explains the Levitical family behind Psalms 42 and 44–49. Planned paintings show deer, water, mountains and anonymous worshipers; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: As the deer pants
verses.heading: Thirst as a picture of longing for God
verses.meaning: The heading names the sons of Korah and calls the psalm a Maskil, probably a song of instruction or skill. The opening image is simple: a deer pants for streams of water. In a dry land, a deer searching for water during drought is a picture of desperate need. The psalmist says his soul longs for God in the same way. The longing is not for an idea about God but for God Himself. The verse begins in need, not in satisfaction.
verses.context: Joel 1:20 pictures wild animals panting for water when streams dry up, and Psalm 63:1 describes thirsting for God in a dry and weary land. Psalm 42:1 opens Book Two with that image.
explore: Pants
The word suggests a strong, almost physical longing. It is not mild interest.
My soul longs
The 'soul' is the whole living person. The desire involves the entire self.
verses.reflect: What are you thirsty for right now? How could that thirst become a prayer for God?
verses.alt: A young deer stretches its neck toward a thin trickle in a dry streambed.

verses.title: The living God
verses.heading: Longing to appear before God
verses.meaning: My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear in God's presence? The speaker calls God 'the living God,' contrasting Him with lifeless idols and suggesting the source of life itself. To 'appear in God's presence' was the language of pilgrimage festivals, when Israel came to the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 16:16). The speaker is far away and cannot go. The question 'When?' shows how long the separation feels. The longing is real, and so is the delay.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 16:16 commands appearing before the LORD three times a year, and Psalm 84:2 says, 'My heart and my flesh cry out for the living God.' Psalm 42:2 voices that desire from a distance.
explore: The living God
God is alive and gives life. The title contrasts Him with idols.
When shall I come?
The question expresses delay and longing. The speaker cannot yet return.
verses.reflect: Where do you feel far from God? What would it mean to ask Him honestly, 'When?'
verses.alt: A distant hilltop sanctuary glows faint on the horizon beyond many ridges.

verses.title: Tears for food
verses.heading: Grief mocked by others
verses.meaning: My tears have been my food both day and night, while men ask me all day long, 'Where is your God?' Grief has replaced appetite. Tears are the speaker's constant diet, day and night. Others add to the pain by mocking his faith: where is this God you trust? Their question implies that God has abandoned him or does not exist. The verse is honest about sorrow and about how others' words can wound faith. It gives permission to grieve while still addressing God.
verses.context: Psalm 79:10 and Joel 2:17 record nations asking, 'Where is their God?' Here the taunt is personal. Psalm 80:5 speaks of God feeding His people the bread of tears.
explore: Tears my food
Grief replaces nourishment. The sorrow is constant.
Where is your God?
The taunt attacks the speaker's trust. It is repeated in verse 10.
verses.reflect: Have others' doubts ever made your grief heavier? How could you bring that question back to God?
verses.alt: An untouched bowl of food sits beside a guttering lamp at night.

verses.title: The festive procession
verses.heading: Memories of worship with the crowd
verses.meaning: These things come to mind as I pour out my soul: how I walked with the multitude, leading the festive procession to the house of God with shouts of joy and praise. Memory now becomes both comfort and pain. The speaker remembers leading a joyful pilgrimage crowd to God's house, a natural role for a Levitical singer. Pouring out the soul is honest grief. Remembering the joyful past shows how much has been lost, but it also reminds him what God's presence is like.
verses.context: Psalm 122:1 says, 'I was glad when they said to me, “Let us go to the house of the LORD”,' and 2 Samuel 6:15 describes David bringing the ark up with shouts. Psalm 42:4 recalls such a procession.
explore: Pour out my soul
The phrase means speaking freely in grief. Hannah used it in 1 Samuel 1:15.
With the multitude
Worship was communal. The speaker misses the crowd as well as the place.
verses.reflect: What memories of joyful worship do you carry? How could they give you hope now?
verses.alt: A crowd with tambourines and palm branches climbs a road toward a temple gate.

verses.title: Why are you downcast?
verses.heading: The first refrain of hope
verses.meaning: Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him for the salvation of His presence. Here the speaker talks to himself. He asks why his soul is sinking and restless, then gives himself an instruction: hope in God. He does not deny the feelings; he answers them. 'I will yet praise Him' expects a future when praise returns. This refrain recurs in 42:11 and 43:5, binding the two psalms together. Hope is chosen while sorrow remains.
verses.context: The same words recur in Psalm 42:11 and 43:5, marking the stanzas of one poem. Lamentations 3:21–24 likewise shows a sufferer recalling God's mercies to find hope.
explore: Talking to the soul
The speaker addresses himself. He answers despair with truth.
I will yet praise
Praise is expected in the future. Hope does not require present relief.
verses.reflect: What would you say to your own soul today if you spoke to it as this psalm does?
verses.alt: A heron stands still at the edge of a grey pond as a thin gap of sunlight opens in the clouds.

verses.title: From the land of Jordan
verses.heading: Remembering God from far away
verses.meaning: O my God, my soul despairs within me. Therefore I remember You from the land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon, even from Mount Mizar. The speaker names where he is: the far north, near the headwaters of the Jordan and the Hermon range. Mount Mizar, meaning 'small mountain,' is unknown. Despite despair, he chooses to remember God from where he is. Distance from the temple does not stop remembrance. The verse is a turning: despair and memory side by side.
verses.context: Mount Hermon rises at Israel's northern border, where springs feed the Jordan (Deuteronomy 3:8–9). The location places the speaker far from Jerusalem, perhaps in exile or flight. Jonah 2:7 shows another distant person remembering the LORD.
explore: Therefore I remember
Despair leads to memory of God. Remembering is an act of faith.
Mount Mizar
The 'small mountain' is unidentified. It emphasizes a lonely, distant place.
verses.reflect: Where are you right now, physically or emotionally? How could you remember God from there?
verses.alt: Snow-capped Mount Hermon rises above green springs feeding a river.

verses.title: Deep calls to deep
verses.heading: Overwhelmed by waves
verses.meaning: Deep calls to deep in the roar of Your waterfalls; all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me. The northern waterfalls near Hermon become an image of being overwhelmed. Water that the deer longed for now crashes over the speaker. 'Deep calls to deep' pictures one roaring wave answering another, an endless sequence. Strikingly, they are 'Your' waterfalls and 'Your' waves: even the overwhelming is within God's world. Jonah 2:3 echoes this line.
verses.context: Jonah 2:3 repeats the line 'all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me' from inside the fish. Psalm 88:7 also describes God's waves overwhelming the sufferer.
explore: Deep calls to deep
One depth answers another. The image is of relentless, overwhelming water.
Your breakers
The waves belong to God. Even the flood is not outside His rule.
verses.reflect: What feels like waves rolling over you? What changes if you see them as within God's reach?
verses.alt: A thundering waterfall plunges into a churning pool between dark cliffs.

verses.title: His song in the night
verses.heading: Love by day and song by night
verses.meaning: The LORD decrees His loving devotion by day, and at night His song is with me as a prayer to the God of my life. In the middle of lament, the covenant name LORD appears, rare in Book Two. God commands His loving devotion like a king issuing a decree. By night, when grief is often worst, a song is with the speaker, becoming prayer. 'The God of my life' names God as the source and keeper of life. The verse is a moment of calm between storms.
verses.context: Job 35:10 speaks of God who gives songs in the night, and Acts 16:25 records Paul and Silas singing at midnight in prison. Psalm 42:8 places such a song in the speaker's own darkness.
explore: Decrees His loving devotion
God commands steadfast love. It is His royal decision.
The God of my life
God is the source of life. The title is personal and trusting.
verses.reflect: What song or prayer could you keep with you through a hard night?
verses.alt: A small lyre rests on a blanket beside a window full of stars.

verses.title: God my Rock
verses.heading: Honest questions to the steady One
verses.meaning: I say to God my Rock, 'Why have You forgotten me? Why must I walk in sorrow because of the enemy's oppression?' The speaker calls God his Rock, a picture of stability, and then asks why He seems to have forgotten. Both are true for the speaker at once: trust and bewilderment. Walking in sorrow describes going about daily life under oppression. The verse models faith that brings hard questions to God rather than away from Him.
verses.context: Psalm 13:1 asks, 'How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?' and Psalm 43:2 repeats this verse's second question. Lament in Scripture often asks God why while still calling Him by trusting names.
explore: God my Rock
God is steady and dependable. The speaker uses that name even while questioning.
Why have You forgotten me?
The question is honest. God's apparent absence is named, not hidden.
verses.reflect: What question would you bring to God your Rock today?
verses.alt: A massive boulder stands firm in a river while rain falls.

verses.title: Like crushing bones
verses.heading: Taunts that hurt like injury
verses.meaning: Like the crushing of my bones, my enemies taunt me, while they say to me all day long, 'Where is your God?' The taunt from verse 3 returns, now described as physical injury. Words hurt like broken bones. The repetition 'all day long' shows how relentless the mockery is. The verse names the real damage that cruel words about faith can cause. It brings that pain to God rather than letting it silence prayer.
verses.context: Proverbs 12:18 says reckless words pierce like a sword, and Psalm 102:8 says, 'All day long my enemies taunt me.' Psalm 42:10 repeats verse 3's taunt with greater force.
explore: Crushing of my bones
The image is of deep, physical pain. Words wound the whole person.
All day long
The mockery does not stop. Its repetition adds to the hurt.
verses.reflect: Have words about your faith ever hurt deeply? How could you bring that injury to God?
verses.alt: Thorny brambles have overgrown a broken stone wall in harsh noon light.

verses.title: My Savior and my God
verses.heading: The refrain returns with a personal ending
verses.meaning: Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God. The refrain returns almost exactly as in verse 5, but ends differently: instead of 'the salvation of His presence,' it says 'my Savior and my God.' The ending is more personal. The sorrow has not vanished, but the speaker again chooses hope. Repetition shows that faith often has to answer despair more than once.
verses.context: Psalm 42:5 and 43:5 frame this verse; the change to 'my Savior and my God' makes the hope personal. Psalm 62:5–6 also addresses the soul and names God as salvation and rock.
explore: Again
The refrain repeats because despair returns. Hope is chosen again.
My Savior and my God
God is named in personal terms. The relationship is the ground of hope.
verses.reflect: Is there a truth you need to tell your soul again today, even if you told it yesterday?
verses.alt: A spring bubbles up between stones as dawn breaks over a valley.
